rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

The six-minute gradient retains full resolution, with the closest pair at R = 2.46. Test the next shorter gradient to reduce runtime while preserving the maximum CRF.
Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The first pair may fall below R = 1.5; the four-minute method remains a fully resolved fallback with maximum CRF.

Test whether higher temperature improves selectivity for the unresolved first pair at the minimum gradient duration. This isolates the temperature effect and may recover full resolution with an even earlier last peak.

Higher temperature worsened the critical separations, so test the lowest available temperature at the same gradient slope. This should favor resolution and establish whether temperature alone can rescue the two-minute gradient.

Reduce gradient steepness at the temperature that best separates the first pair, aiming to lift its resolution above 1.5. The last compound will likely elute during the final hold, allowing a short gradient without sacrificing early-pair resolution.

Shift the successful two-minute gradient window upward while preserving its slope and temperature. This tests whether stronger final solvent can accelerate the last peak while retaining full resolution of the first pair.

Shift the gradient window upward another 0.10 at unchanged slope, which preserved full resolution in the previous shift. The stronger endpoint should shorten the final hold, while this run tests whether the first pair remains sufficiently retained and resolved.

The fastest fully resolved method so far is injection 11, but its first pair has little resolution margin. Lower the endpoint one step to flatten the gradient and seek a more robust maximum-CRF method with only a modest increase in final-peak retention.
